†*364. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: Will the Minister of 
PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government are seriously considering to restore the right to fix 
domestic retail prices of petrol and diesel to the oil companies; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) by when a final decision is likely to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (c) Since th e end of 2003, there has been an 
unprecedented, sharp and spiraling incr ease in international oil prices 
combined with considerable week-to-week and even day-to-day volatility. The 
Indian basket of crude oil touched an all-time high of US $ 52.83 per bbl on 04-
04-2005 compared to an average price of US $ 27.96 per bbl in 2003-04 and US 
$ 39.21 per bbl in 2004-05. There has since been some 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
12 

[19 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
softening, the Indian basket having declined to around US $ 47/bbl in the week 
ending 16.4.2005. 
With a view to-containing the burden of the increase in international prices 
on consumers of diesel and petrol, it was decided that the burden should be 
equitably shared also by the Government and Oil Companies. Thus, 
Government reduced the excise duty on petrol and diesel by 4% and 3% 
respectively effective 16.6.04. Effective 19.8.04, the excise duty on petrol and 
diesel was further reduced by 3%. The Government also reduced customs duty 
by 5% each on petrol and diesel with effect from 19/8/04. In the Budget 2005-
06, a reduction in custom duty on crude from 10% to 5% and in other petroleum 
products from 15-20% to 10% was announced. 
Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) have not passed on the full 
increase in international prices to the domestic consumer prices of these products. 
Although, with effect from 1st August 2004, Government had worked out a price 
band mechanism, allowing OMCs freedom to revise the prices of petrol and diesel 
within the prescribed price band, the steep and volatile increase in the 
international prices of crude oil resulted in the ceiling of the price band being 
breached within weeks of its being made operational resulting in the 
mechanism being placed in abeyance. 
The pricing mechanism attempts to balance the interests of various 
stakeholders, viz., Consumers, Government and Oil Companies. The burden 
borne by oil companies will, of course, go up to the extent that domestic 
prices are not revised upwards when international prices shoot up, but it is hoped 
that when international prices stabilize, or Government so decides, the price band 
mechanism might be restored. It may be noted that private sector companies are 
free to fix their prices.

(c) what action has been taken by Government thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI PRIYARANJAN 
DASMUNSI): (a) to (c) The Government of India had set up a Task Force for Flood 
Management/Erosion control under the chairmanship of Chairman, CWC to look into 
the problem of floods in Assam & neighbouring states, West Bengal, Bihar & Eastern 
Uttar Pradesh in August, 2004. The Task Force has submitted its report on 31.12.2004 
to Ministry of Water Resources. The broad recommendations of the Task Force are as 
under:— 
The Task Force has recommended expanding the role of the Central Government in 
the flood control sector. It has recommended that the flood control schemes should be 
funded through the Centrally Sponsored Scheme in the ratio of 90% Central and 10% 
State from the present 75:25. The Task Force has recommended that corpus for Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme also needs to be increased substantially to accommodate all critical 
flood management and critical anti-erosion works. 
The Task Force has recommended schemes worth Rs. 316.14 crore as immediate 
measures to be taken before the coming flood season. The Schemes worth Rs. 2030.15 
crore have been recommended during the remaining two years of the 10th Five Year Plan i.e. 
during the 2005-06 and 2006-07 under short term-l measures and Rs. 2635.81 crore have 
been estimated as requirment during the 11th Plan. 
Task Force has recommended that the investment for plan/Flood Management 
may be increased from the existing half per cent of the total outlay to at least 1%. 
 It has recommended earmarking funds in the total State sector as Additional 
Central assistance for maintenance of embankments. 
Eligibility criteria for Central funding is proposed to be reduced to Rs. 1 crore from the 
existing limit of Rs. 3 crore per scheme. 
The Task-Force has recommended creation of a revolving fund of say Rs. 50 crore 
which may be available annually to the Ministry of Water Resources to take up 
emergent flood management schemes. The normal

requirement of 'in principle' approval of Planning Commission is recommended to 
be waived in this particular case. The schemes under this fund could be implemented by 
the States/Board after inspection by CWC/Brahmaputra Board. The Task Force has further 
recommended that to mobilize resources for this revolving fund, a flood cess of say 1 % to 
2% could be levied on new infrastructures like roads, buildings, power plants etc. in the 
flood prone States. 
The Task Force has recommended that the Central Government may consider funding 
the flood control component of the reservoir projects. 
Under the institutional arrangements, the Task Force has recommended setting up of an 
Authority in the North East region with all the statutory powers. In the meantime it 
has recommended strengthening and restructuring of the Brahmaputra Board. 
The Task Force has recommended establishment of Sikkim and North Bengal River 
Management Board as well as strengthening of the Ganga Flood Control Commission by 
addition of a Member (Works) and appropriate field formations for investigation and execution 
of critical flood management works. 
The Task Force has recommended extension of jurisdiction of Farakka Barrage

In order to have policy formulation and coordination among various agencies so 
recommended by the Task Force, it has also recommended strengthening of Flood 
Management Organizations of the Central Water Commission by re-starting the post of 
Member (Floods) abolished earlier and re-deployment of posts of Chief Engineer, two 
Directors and other lower level functionaries. 
The Task Force has also recommended that the Brahmaputra Board and the proposed 
Sikkim and North Bengal River Management Board be entrusted the techno-economical 
examination of the schemes for submission to the Planning Commission for

Discriminatory pricing of gulf crude 
*372. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that many developing countries in South-East Asia 
are paying additional premium for gulf crude to the extent of $2.00 per barret 
(b) if so, whether India and other affected countries have taken up the matter 
of discriminatory pricing of crude with the OPEC nations; and 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
(c) the quantum of additional premium India had to pay during the year 
2004-05 on this account?  
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) Most West Asian countries sell their crude oil at their 
Official Selling Price (OSP). The OSPs vary from destination to destination, largely 
because of differing degrees of competition in the market. There being well-organized 
petroleum and petroleum products markets in North America and West Europe, with West 
Texas Intermediate (WTI) and Brent (dated) as well-recognized markers, buyers in 
these markets often secure a discount not available in less well-organized markets. 
Yet, it is not always that OSPs in these markets are lower than elsewhere. Thus, for part 
of 2004-05, the OSP for Asian countries was higher than that of Europe and USA and 
for the rest of the year, it was lower. The Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas and 
Panchayati Raj, Government of India, highlighted this in his keynote address to the OPEC 
International Seminar titled "Petroleum in an Interdependent World" held in Vienna in 
September, 2004. The issue was also raised in the First Round Table of Asian Oil 
Ministers on Stability, Security and Sustainability through Regional Cooperation headed by 
India in New Delhi on 6th January, 2005. The relevant conclusion of the Round Table, as 
set out in the Chairman's concluding remarks is reproduced below: 
(1) There is scope for improving Asian markets for petroleum and petroleum 
products. The issue requires careful study and detailed consideration, primarily 
among experts and operators with a view to identifying broad policy parameters 
that might require further consideration. 
(2) Prices should be sustained at levels which encourage Asian consumers to 
increase their purchase of Asian produce; at the same time, prices should be such as 
to encourage Asian producers to promote investment in oil and gas for Asian 
consumer destinations as an economic priority. 
(c) Since a number of grades of crude oil are marketed by these countries to different 
regions, it is difficult to estimate exactly the quantum of the premium for a particular 
region vis-a-vis other regions. Moreover, it is also variable from time to time.'

The action taken by the Government/Public Sector Oil Marketing

New European regulations for Airlines 
2786. SHRI T.S. BAJWA: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to refer to the 
answer to Unstarred Question 9 given in the Rajya Sabha on the 1st March, 2005 and 
state: 
(a) whether the law or similar law will be applicable to the domestic airlines; and 
(b) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI 
PRAFUL PATEL): (a) and (b) There is presently no proposal to enact a law in line with 
the regulation adopted by European Union (EU) providing for compensation and 
assistance to air passengers in the event of denied boarding the cancellation or long delay 
of flights. The present international air law as established by Warsaw Convention and 
Montreal Convention 1999 envisage only a measure of facilitation and do not 
contemplate any punitive action against airlines. Most airlines in India 
38 

[19 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
already have procedures in place for pr oviding standard passenger facilitation 
measures in the event of delay/postponement of flights and do everything within their 
means to ensure that stranded passengers are not inconvenienced. Besides, because of the very 
nature of the air transportation industry, safety considerations have to be given foremost 
priority and reasons for delay of the flights are often beyond the control of the airlines. Such 
a punitive law may also end up increasing the cost of air travel considerably as airlines 
may be compelled to pass on a part of the financial burden to the passengers.

Amendment of VAT system 
†2841. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are bent upon implementing VAT' 
without full consent of State Governments; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that tr aders from all over the country are 
agitating on being suspicious of VAT; 
(c) if so, the reasons for adopting adamant attitude instead of finding 
peaceful solution of this matter by Government; and 
(d) whether Government is considering to amend the present form of VAT' 
in view of country-wide protest? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) VAT is a State level tax reform measure, 
which was implemented with effect from 1st April, 2005 by most of the 
States. An Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers has been set up 
to decide on all issues relating to implementation of State level VAT. The 
Empowered Committee of State Finance Ministers has decided to implement 
VAT and has finalized the VAT design, after prolonged deliberations and due 
consideration of advantages offered by the VAT system and concerns of all 
stakeholders including traders. Therefore, the question of Government of India 
being bent upon implementation of VAT without full consent of the State 
Governments does not arise. 
(b) to (d) It is true that a section of the trading community is agitating against 
VAT. As State level VAT is a State subject, any decision to amend the present 
form of VAT is to be taken by the Empowered Committee of the State Finance 
Ministers. The Empowered Committee is seized of the issue and is looking into 
the genuine problems/concerns of traders.

S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): Prior to 1.4.2003, total exemption was available to

ports may also take advantage of this provision.

including ports is proposed to be made available to enterprises owned by an 
authority or board or a corporation or any other body established or constituted 
under any central or State act also, it is expected that the State Maritime 
Boards operating ports would be cushioned against any adverse financial 
impact.

Section 80-IA, no specific revenue is targeted from the Gujarat Port Authorities in

2872. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO:  Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government  are seriously considering to relax

Corporates to raise borrowing from overseas; 
(c) whether any time-frame has been fixe d by which these restrictions are 
going to be relaxed; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) As announced in the Budget 2005-06, 
window has been opened to enable qualified NGOs engaged in micro-finance 
to access the External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) window. 
(b) As per extant guidelines, all cor porates registered under the Companies 
Act, 1956 except financial intermediaries, are eligible borrowers under the 
automatic route for ECBs up to USD 500 million. Proposals not covered under 
the automatic route are considered by a committee set up by RBI. Financial 
institutions dealing exclusively with infrastructure or export finance can raise 
ECB through the approval route. Banks and financial institutions which had 
participated in the textile or steel sector restructuring package as approved by the 
Government will also be permitted to the extent of their investment in the 
package and assessment by RBI based on prudential norms. 
ECB can be raised only for investment (such as import of capital goods, 
new projects, modernization/expansion of existing production units) in real sector,

Statement-I 
The Inaugural Address of Chairman of Round Table Conference 
Your Excellency, the co-host of this conclave, the distinguished Head of 
Delegation of the Emirate of Kuwait, 
Your Excellencies, Ministers and Heads of Delegation from the principal Asian 
suppliers and consumers of petroleum, 
Your Excellencies, Ambassadors to New Delhi of these countries, 
Distinguished representatives of the Governments of participating countries, 
Distinguished representatives of National Oil Companies and the Asian Oil 
Industry, 
Distinguished delegates of the principal international organizations here 
present, our co-sponsor, the Secretary-General of the International Energy Forum, 
the distinguished representative of the International Energy Agency, and the 
distinguished Acting Secretary-General of OPEC-the Organisation of Petroleum 
Exporting Countries, 
My fellow-Minister, the distinguished Minister of State of External Affairs of 
India, Shri E. Ahamed, Ladies and Gentlemen, Fellow Asians, 
We meet in the shadow of the terrible Tsunami tragedy that has struck our shared 
continent of Asia. May l request you to please and observe a minute's silence in 
memory of the 125,000 or more who have been snatched so cruelly from our 
midst?... 
Thank you. 
This is the moment that might yet be recorded as "historic" in the annals of 
regional cooperation in Asia. For this is  the first gathering together of the 
principal Asian ministers charged with responsibility for the most crucial 
sector of the economy-petroleum and natural gas. Whether our meeting today 
does get recorded as "historic" does, of course, depend on the outcome of our 
deliberations and of our resolves to persist on the path of such dialogue. I have 
little doubt, however, that it will-for in the very act 
139 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
of journeying to our capital you have registered your commitment to our shared 
destiny. Through almost all of the advancement of human civilization, it is Asia that 
has been in the vanguard. For the last few centuries, we fell to the sway of others. 
Now, once again, we are the captains of our ship and the masters of our fate. I 
thank you most warmly and sincerely, on behalf of our Government and all our 
one billion people, for having done us the unforgettable honour of being present 
here at the creation. Thank you, indeed. 
Excellencies, in the sector of our concern, hydrocarbons, the dawn of the 21st 
century heralds an unprecedented, dare I say revolutionary change in international 
oil and gas relations. In the last quarter of the last century, Asian oil producers 
came into their own when OPEC secured fair and just remuneration for the most 
vital element of growth and prosperity-oil. Now has come Asia's turn to consume 
that oil and thus fuel the resurgence of Asia as the harbinger of the further 
advancement of human civilization. The total consumption of the Asian 
countries here present almost equals the total production of the Asian countries 
here present. No longer are we labouring so that others might profit. We have 
already emerged as the world's principal source of supply, we are emerging as the 
world's principal destination for the consumption of that supply. Already, some two 
thirds of the fossil fuel that principal producers around this table extract from 
the bosom of Mother Nature is brought by the principal consumers represented at 
this very table. That trend will only accelerate as we traverse the 21st century-
the Asian Century. We are gathered here to rise to that challenge and to avail of 
that opportunity. 
The Challenge, Your excellencies, lies in eschewing the errors of the past. The 
opportunity,Your Excellencies, lies in Fashioning a more fair,; more just and 
more remunerative oil order for all of us in Asia-in which the Asian producer is 
ensured a stable, secure and sustainable return for a most precious but depleting 
natural resource and the Asian consumer is assured a stable, secure and sustainable 
regime within which to promote progress and prosperity for that deprived one-
half of humankind that inhabits our shared continent of Asia. We commence 
here a dialogue to meet that challenge and rise to that opportunity. 
How do we do so? 
First let me deal with stability. Last year has seen the worst roller-coaster- 
140 

[19 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
ride in oil prices for the better part of a generation. OPEC has behaved most 
responsibly through this period of turmoil and turbulence. Instead of pursuing 
short-term advantage, OPEC, led by its Asian members, has persistently striven 
for moderating volatility and dampening speculation. For this, OPEC and its 
membership have earned the world's gratitude. Moreover, OPEC'S production 
plans give the world the reassurance that global oil supply will keep pace with 
booming global demand, and that over the next twenty years at least there will 
be no market disequilibrium to warrant any wild fluctuation in prices. If, 
nevertheless, volatility rather than stability has marked international prices in 
the last twelve months that is largely because of speculation and apprehensions-
that have been mostly belied-of the fallout on oil production of exogenous 
political developments. The fact is that however uncertain developments in the 
world political order have been, the underlying global oil economy has held a 
steady course. 
For us in Asia to convert that underlying stability in production (and the 
prognosis for production) into stability in oil markets, it is essential that we 
develop as sophisticated Asian market for petroleum and petroleum products. 
That is how the West converted their abundance of natural resources into 
abundance of production and consumption. 
Unfortunately, we in Asia continue to behave as if we were still a residual 
consumer of Asian oil production when, in fact, we are the principal 
consumer. 
Your Excellencies, for Asia to be the residual consumer made some economic 
sense when there was large and growing production on both sides of the 
Atlantic, on-land in the America and off-shore in Europe. It was in that era that 
Western Texas Intermediate (WTI) and Brent emerged as makers. But as the 
world wheels into the 21st century, WTI output is down by three-quarter 
compared to two decades ago and Brent output is down by two-third compared to 
just a decade ago-and both are set decline even further, and to decline quite 
precipitately at that. Meanwhile, it is Asia, from Eastern Siberia through the 
Caspian, Central Asia and China, to South-East Asia and to come extent even 
South Asia and of course, above alt, Iran and West Asia, that is booming in 
both and output and throughput of oil. yet, Asia has littele in terms of global 
marker. And even less in terms of a well-prepared oil and oil products market. 
141 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
With a view to bringing about greater stability in Asian trade in petroleum and 
petroleum products, can we think in term of an Asian market. 
* where long-term contracts become longer, 
* where price discovery through the market in more transparent, 
* where such transparency facilitates greater stability in formulate for 
pricing in long-term contracts, 
* where spot purchases occupy a progressively larger share of market 
transactions, 
* where petroleum exchanges are establishes and used, 
* where derivatives are integrated into market practice, 
* where, in short, an Asian marker emerges 
which reflects Asian realities and the real role in the global oil economy of Asian 
production, Asian consumption and Asian trade? 
To pose the problem, Your Excellencies, is easier than to find the answers. But I do 
submit, Your Excellencies, that through sustained dialogue among ourselves, 
buttressed by dialogue among our experts and market operators, we might be able 
to find an Asian solution to the imperatives of Asian stability. 
As for the second theme of our meeting-security-the answer there too lies in 
promoting mutual interdependence. Security has two aspects. One is security 
against unexpected disruption of supplies. As a joint emergency reponse 
mechanism, perhaps we should consider jointly building storages which would 
enable consumers to enjoy an uninterrupted flow of supplies and producers to 
enjoy an uninterrupted flow of oil revenue till normalcy is restored. 
The second aspect of security relates to assurance of markets for producers and 
assurance of supplies for consumers. Th is calls for mutual interdependence 
through mutual investments in each other's countries by producer and consumer 
nations of the Asian oil community. Hitherto, we have looked West for much of 
the investment in Asian petroleum exploration and production, Asian petroleum 
refining, and Asian petroleum marketing-and in saying so I include gas as well. 
Now, increasingly, Asian itself is 
142 

[19 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
merging as a significant source of investment in Asia. Japan, is of course, a long-
established Asian investor in other Asian countries. China in the last decade, as 
also Malaysia, have beocme key players, in E&P in Asia and, indeed, the world 
over. So has India. We are already in E&P refining and marketing projects in more 
than ten countries and much of our overseas investment is in Asia, reciprocally, in 
refining, we in India have been the beneficiary of investments by Iran in the 
Chennai Petroleum Corporation and of Qatar in LNG These are but illustrative 
examples. A future beckons in which Asian countries can become major 
participants in the massive investments which need to be made in the Asian 
countries represented at this table, running to an estimated 1580 billion dollars 
over the next 25 years in upstream, midstream and downstream oil and gas 
development in all our countries put together. Investment on this humungous 
scale, to the extent possible mutual and reciprocal intra-Asia investment, 
would hugely enhance security of production and consumption for all of us around 
this table, for all our fellow-Asians and, indeed, for all of humankind the world 
over. The oil and gas sector in India welcomes the world with open arms, and 
reserves a particular welcome for Asian investors. Equally, we stand ready to do 
our share for the promotion of the global oil economy in general and the Asian 
oil economy in particular. We believe we should continue and intensify this 
dialogue in the interests of facilitating mutual investments to ensure mutual 
security. 
The third great theme of our meeting today is sustainability. It has taken 
millions of years, indeed, hundreds of millions of years for Nature to create and 
storewhat we have substantially exhausted in a mere one hundred years or so. 
What remains we can use only if used with great care. That calls for 
conservation, on the one hand, and technology, on the other. Japan has shown 
the way to both conservation and the technology for conservation, as perhaps no 
other country in the world has. India has had no alternative but to conserve and 
innovate, although we still have a long, long way to go. China has taken significant 
initiatives. So has the Republic of Korea. Asian oil exporting countries have 
demonstrated a commendable awareness of the importance of sustainability. The 
time now is for us to pool together ou r experience, forge th em into a shared, 
common experience, and build on that e xperience in concert. Sustainability in 
Asia calls for sustained dialogue among Asians. We stand ready and willing to 
place our Petroleum Conservation Research Association, the Indian Institute

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
of Petroleum, the University of Petroleum Studies, The Energy and Research institute of India 
(TERI), our Centre for High Technology, our Oil Industry Safety Directorate, Indian Oil's 
R&D Centre, and all our other scientific and technological research and development 
institutions at the service of all Asia. It is said that one in every three Information 
Technologists in the world is an Indian. Our achievement in petroleum technology is 
perhaps less spectacular. But we would be more than happy to share what we know with 
our fellow-Asians and even more to learn from others, above all to learn from our fellow-

As we embark on this historic initiative which will, I hope, bring us together frequently, even 
up to once or preferably twice a year, perhaps alternately in a net oil exporting and a net oil 
importing country of Asia, and perhaps progressively; expanding our ambit while keeping our 
core intact, I welcome all of you once again to our national capital and wish you all a

Your Exellencies, I thank you, one and all. 
Statement-II 
Chairman's Statement on the conclusion of the first round Table of Asian Ministers on 
Regional Cooperation in the Oil and Gas economy, New Delhi on 6th January, 
2006. 
A. GENERAL 
1. The Asian oil economy is integral to, and inseparable from, the global oil economy. 
2. With Asian destinations emerging as the principal consumers for Asian 
production, and the share of Asia in global production and consumption likely to 
progressively increase, cooperation between Asian producers and Asian consumers is 
crucial to ensuring— 
Stability, 
Security and 
Sustainability 
through 
144 

[19 April, 2005]        RAJYA SABHA 
mutual interdependence 
in the Asian Oil and Gas economy. 
3. The fundamentals of such cooperation must include moderation, dialogue, 
mutual understanding and respect, security of international supplies, demand-supply 
equilibrium, and strategic partnererships based on a reciprocity of interests. 
4. To this end, an Asian dialogue is both welcome and indispensable aimed at 
evolving and elaborating an Asian concensus. 
5. It is, therefore, agreed that the instrumentality of Round Tables of Asian 
Ministers on Regional Cooperation in the Oil and Gas Economy, initiated here in New 
Delhi, must be maintained. The following countries have kindly agreed to host/co-host 
subsequent Round Tables: 
Second Round Table                    : Saudi Arabia, 
Co-host: Japan 
Third Round Table                         : Japan, 
Co-Host: Qatar 
Fourth Round Table                     : Kuwait, 
Co-host: Republic of Korea 
The Round Tables may follow the pattern of alternating between net importing and net 
exporting countries. 
6. For the preparation of Ministerial Round Tables, the Secretariat of the 
International Energy Forum might convene experts, operators and officials to prepare 
position papers and agenda documents. 
7. To reinforce Ministerial-level discussions at the Round Tables, a parallel; effort 
may be initiated to bring together Asian business operators belonging to the countries 
represented at the Round Table. 
B. STABILITY AND SECURITY 
1. There is scope for improving Asian markets for petroleum and petroleum 
products. The issue requires careful study and detailed consideration, primarily 
among experts and operators with a view to identifying broad policy parameters that might 
require further consideration. 
2. Prices should be sustained at levels which encourage Asian 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
consumers to increase their purchases of Asian produce at the same time, 
prices should be such as to encourage Asian producers to promote investment in 
oil and gas for Asian consumer destinations as an economic priority. 
3. Crisscross investments all along th e entire oil and gas products chain 
through reciprocal investment interlocking of producers and consumers will 
guarantee security of both supply and demand, thus contributing to stability of 
prices and thereby security of both supply and demand. Thus stability of prices 
would encourage domestic and crosscountry investment in all streams of the 
petroleum sector and other energy-related projects. 
4. Caution must be exercised in promoting balanced investment so that 
over-investment does not lead to excess capacity nor under-investment to shortage 
of supplies. 
5. Strategic storage and stockpiling contribute to security, and in this regard 
the valuable experience of Japan might hold significant lessons for other major 
consumers. However, there must be  no abuse for illegitimate commercial 
purposes of such strategic storage and stockpiles. 
6. the exchange of information and knowledge is the key to increasing 
confidence on the part of both buyers and sellers. 
7. The Sustainable and Flexible Energy system (SAFE) proposed by Japan 
constitutes a useful framework for further consideration of issues of energy 
security. 
8. The Iranian proposal for an Asian Bank for energy Development merits 
deeper consideration. 
C.SUSTAINABILITY 
1. Endorsing the importance of energy conservation for the protection of the 
environment and issues of climate change, the need for technological cooperation in 
the pursuit of cleaner and more environmentally-sound fossil fuel; technologies 
was emphasized.

Import of crude from Saudi Arabia on long term basis 
2907. SHRI MURLI DEORA: Will th e Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Western countries are normally importing crude from Saudi 
153 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
Arabia at lower price than the prices paid by Asian countries; 
(b) whether India is proposing to have an option to choose the benchmark at 
which it would import the crude by entering into long term oil contracts; 
(c) if so, the response of Saudi Arabian Government to the proposal; and 
(d) the financial benefit to be accorded to Indian oil economy by this price 
stability and supply security formula? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) Most West Asian countries including Saudi Arabia sell their 
crude oil at their Official Selling Price (OSP). The OSPs vary from destination to 
destination, largely because of differing degrees of competition in the market. There 
being well-organized petroleum and petroluem products markets in North America 
and West Europe, with West Texas Intermediate (WTI) and Brent (dated) as well-
recognized markers, buyers in these markets often secure a discount not available in less 
well-organized markets. Yet, it is not always that OSPs in these markets are lower 
than elsewhere. Thus, for part of 2004-05, the OSP for Asian countries was higher than 
that of Europe and USA and for the rest of the year, it was lower. 
(b) to (d) More than two-thirds of the imported crude in India comes from West 
Asian countries where prices are fixed at the Official Selling Price (OSP). The rest of 
the crude is procured on spot basis through tenders floated by PSUs. Thus, India 
deles not have the option of choosing the marker crude. In view of this, the 
question of the development of an Asian Petroleum and Petroleum Products 
Market was discussed at the First Round Table of Asian Oil Ministers on 
Stability, Security and Sustainability through Regional Cooperation in New Delhi on 
6 January, 2005. Saudi Arabia has supported the proposal for a study to be done on the 
development of the Asian Petroleum and Petroleum Products Market.

Unfair trade practices of RIL 
2908. SHRI CHITTABRATA MAJUMDAR: Will the Minister of 
PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether M/s IOCL in November, 2004 complained to Government 
regarding unfair trade practice followed by M/s RlL for marketing of diesel 
transported from Jamnagar refinery for sale in their retail outlets in Nagpur area in 
Maharashtra; 
(b) if so, the details of the complaint; and 
(c) the action taken by Government so far? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (c) Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) had reported to the 
Government in November, 2004 that M/s Reliance Industries Ltd. (RIL) bring their 
product from Jamnagar Refinery on stock transfer basis to their retail outlets in the 
Nagpur marketing area in Maharashtra without any tax implications. From these 
retail outlets, diesel is supplied to vehicles operating under M/s Reliance 
Logistics Limited (RLL), a sister concern of RIL for transportation purposes. 
This supply is not shown as sales but as internal consumption by the vehicles 
operating under M/s RLL. Thus, no sales tax is paid on such sales and, 
therefore, the vehicles operating under M/s RLL get diesel at relatively lower 
rates. 
According to IOC, the aforesaid a rrangement of supply to vehicles 
operating under M/s RLL is allegedly being misused as even transporters not 
operating under M/s RLL have been able to get their tanks filled from M/s RIL's 
outlets without paying sales tax. 
Since this issue relates to alleged evasion of sales tax, the matter has been 
brought to the notice of the Government of Maharashtra for appropriate 
action.

Management of irrigation and drinking water 
2929. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of WATER

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) and (b) Water 
being a State subject, water resources projects including schemes on irrigation 
and drinking water are planned, implemented, funded and managed by the respective 
State Governments as per their priorities. However, the issue related to 
management are duly addressed in the National Water Policy. Relevant paras 
are as under:— 
9.1 Irrigation planning either in an individual project or in a basin as a 
whole should take into account th e irrigability of land, cost-
effective irrigation options possible from all available sources 
of water and appropriate irrigation techniques for optimizing 
water use efficiency. Irrigation intensity should be such as to 
extend the benefits of irrigation to as large a number of farm 
families as possible, keeping in view the need 
178 

[19 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
to maximize production. 
9.2 There should be a close integration of water-use and land-use policies. 
9.3 Water allocation in an irrigation system should be done with due regard to 
equity and social justice. Disparities in the availability of water between 
head-reach and tail-end farms and between large and small farms should 
be obviated by adoption of a rotational water distribution system and 
supply of water on a volumetric basis subject to certain ceiling and 
rational pricing. 
9.4 Concerted efforts should be made to ensure that the irrigation potential 
created is fully utilized. For this purpose, the command area 
development approach should be adopted in all irrigation projects. 
9.5 Irrigation being the largest consumer of fresh water, the aim should be to 
get optimal productivity per unit of water. Scientific water 
management, farm practices and sprinkler and drip irrigation should be 
adopted wherever feasible. 
9.6 Reclamation of water logged/saline affected land by scientific and cost-
effective methods should form a part of command area development 
programme. 
 
11. Besides creating additional water resources facilities for various uses, 
adequate emphasis needs to be given to the physical and financial 
sustainability of existing facilities. There is, therefore, a need to ensure that 
the water charges for various uses should be fixed in such a way that they 
cover at least the operation and maintenance charges of providing the 
service initially and a part of the capital costs subsequently. These 
rates should be linked directly to the quality eg off service provided. The 
subsidy on water rates to the disadvantaged and poorer sections of the 
society should be well targeted and transparent. 
12. Management of the water resources for divers uses should incorporate a 
participatory approach; by involving not only the various governmental 
agencies but also the users and other stakeholders, in an effective and 
decisive manner, in various aspects of planning, design, development 
and management of the water resources schemes. Necessary

Water Users Associations and the local bodies such as

involved in the operation, maintenance and management of water 
infrastructures/facilities at appr opriate levels progressively, 
with a view to eventually tran sfer the management of such 
facilities to the user groups/local bodies. The Government of India 
encourages improvements in water management practices. The

Rain water harvesting 
2931. SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that several Civil Society Organizations working in the Water 
Sector had agitation on World Water Day for clean water, quality water, better water 
supply and community rights over water; and 
(b) whether Government are taking steps for rain water harvesting in view of the 
water scarcity in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAY PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Government is aware of 
press reports to the effect that some people staged rally on World Water Day for clean 
water, better water supply etc. 
(b) 'Water' being a State subject, it is primarily the responsibility of the concerned State 
Governments to formulate plans for augmenting water resources. However, the following 
steps have been taken by the Union Government to encourage rain water 
harvesting:- 
(i) Central Ground Water Board (CGWB)' under the Ministry of Water Resources has 
proposed a scheme at an estimated cost of Rs. 175 crores for Artificial 
Recharge to Ground Water and Rain Water Harvesting during the remaining part 
of the Tenth Five Year Plan. 
(ii) Circulation of Manual/Guidelines on Artificial Recharge of Ground Water to the 
States/Union Territories to enable them to formulate area specific artificial 
recharge schemes to check the declining trend of ground water levels. 
(iii) Central Ministries/Departments of Railways, Defence, Posts,            
Telecommunications, Central Public Works Department and National 
Highways Authority of India have been requested to provide  roof top rain water 
harvesting structures in the buildings under  their control. 
(iv) States/UTs have been requested to provide water harvesting structures in 
buildings under their administrative control. 
(v) All the States/Union Territories have been requested for advising the local bodies 
in the respective States/Union Territories to allow 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
rebate in property tax to persons, who adopt roof top rain water 
harvesting in their premises. 
(vi) CGWB has provided technical guidance on rain water harvesting to 
around 1800 agencies, including State Government agencies, 
educational institutions, private entrepreneurs and individuals. 
(vii) Lanuching of a website on Roof Top Rain Water Harvesting 
(www.cgwb.net) to make aware and educate the public about various 
techniques of harvesting rainwater and store it for future use. 
(viii) Organisation of mass awareness program mes and training courses on 
rainwater harvesting and artificial recharge of ground water. 
(ix) Rain Water Harvesting campaign has been launched keeping in view 
the various target groups like youth and children, women, farmers and 
villagers, policy and opinion makers. Publicity through print media, 
telecasting of spots on the television, broadcasting messages on radio, 
holding of seminars, workshops, conferences etc., have been 
undertaken for the purpose. 
(x) The Ministry of Urban Development & Poverty Alleviation, 
Government of India have amended Building Bye-laws, 1983, 
making provision for water harvesting through storing of water run-off 
including rain water in all new buildings on plots of 100 square meters 
and above in Delhi mandatory, similarly, State Governments of Tamil 
Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana, Rajasthan and Kerala have 
made roof top rain water harvesting mandatory in specified cases.

Regional benches of Supreme Court 
*342. SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: Will the Minister of LAW AND 
JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact the that Indian Council of Jurists and the All India Bar 
Association have urged the Supreme Court to reconsider its decision against 
setting up regional benches of Apex Court in Chennai, Kolkata and Mumbai; 
and 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI HANSRAJ BHARDWAJ): 
(a) and (b) According to information received from the Supreme Court of India, 
no request has been received by them from the Indian Council of Jurists and the 
All India Bar Association to reconsider its decision against setting up of regional 
benches of Apex Court in Chennai, Kolkata and Mumbai. 
According to article 130 of the Constitution, "the Supreme Court shall sit in 
Delhi or in such other place or places as the Chief Justice of India may, with the 
approval of the President, from time to time, appoint." However, the Chief Justice of 
India as well as the Full Court have been consistently opposed to the proposal for 
setting up of Benches of the Supreme Court in the South and other regions of the 
country.

*350. SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the State Governments have any control on monitoring and 
regulation of the engineering colleges including issuing No Objection 
Certificate for new colleges; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, whether there is any monitoring and regulatory procedure/ 
mechanism to ensure that various States are not saddled and mushroomed with sub-
standard Engineering colleges; 
(d) if so, the details thereof as on date; and 
(e) the details of the engineering college s and the approved annual intake 
of students in various States for the last three years, year-wise, category-wise 
and State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (d) The All Indi a Council for Tec hnical Education 
(AICTE) takes into account the recommendations and the objections, if any, of 
the respective State Government while deciding the establishment of new 
institutions, an increase in intake as well as adding new programmes in the existing 
institutions of technical education. All the applicants are required to submit 
the proposals simultaneously to the AICTE, the concerned State Governments 
and the affiliating Universities. The AICTE conducts visits by a committee of 
experts to verify the proposals with regard to the facilities and resources 
available in the institutions. Annual visits are undertaken by the committee of 
experts to monitor the quality of education. The State Governments are 
requested to depute their representative at the time of inspection and provide the 
State Government's point of view. Based on the approval of the AICTE for the 
new institution, the State Governments and the affiliating universities are 
responsible for the admission of students. 
Complaints regarding malpractice by institutions are dealt with by the 
Malpractice Prevention Cell of the AICT E and appropriate penal action such 
as a reduction in intake, placing the institutions under the 'no-

Claim over Taj Mahal 
2626. SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: Will the Minister of CULTURE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact they many organisations are making claims over Taj Mahal; and 
228 

[19 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof and Government's response thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Yes, Sir. The Uttar 
Pradesh Sunni Central Wakf Board has issued a notice for registration of Maqbara 
Shahjahan and Mumtaj Mahal property known as "Taj Mahal, Agra" under the provision of 
Section 36 of the Wafk Act, 1995. (Central Act 43 of 1995) 
(b) Archaeological Survey of India is of the view that any attempt of registration of 
Taj Mahal as wakf property by way of issuance of the notice is absolutely illegal, without 
jurisdiction and contrary to the provision of the said Act. The Central Government has a 
sovereign right to possess and manage centrally protected monuments and sites of 
national importance in the country and the authorities of the Wafk Board can not 
interfere with the same. 
Under the provision of the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act, 1904, the preliminary 
notification No. 1412M dated 18.11.1920 was published in the United Provinces Gazette 
on 20th November, 1920 and the final notification was issued vide No. 1645M/1133 dated 
22.12.1920 to declare Taj Mahal, Agra as a protected monuments. 
The Taj Mahal, Agra is not only a centrally protected monument and a cultural heritage 
of national importance but also has been declared by UNESCO as a World Heritage 
Site.

(a) whether it is a fact that NT Delhi has develop a passenger Car Engine 
which will run on bio-diesel fuel after modification in the existing diesel 
engines; 
(b) whether the new technology can be used to run pumps sets and tractors 
for agriculture use; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
 
238

[19 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether the bio-diesel fuel would be cheaper than the diesel presently used to 
run the engines; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEAVY INDUSTRIES 
AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) As per 
information received from Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources, that 
Ministry has sponsored a R&D project to Indian Institute of Techology, Delhi for 
production of bio-diesel from non-edible oil and field trials of diesel car with bio-
diesel operation. Pungamia oil is being studied for production of bio-diesel and its 
effect on the performance of diesel engine. 
According to Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources, IIT, Delhi has 
been able to utilize bio-diesel produced from non-edible oil at a laboratory scale in a 
passenger car. No modifications in the existing diesel engine of the passenger car 
is required if an appropriate quality of bio-diesel is used. 
(b) Bio-diesel blended with diesel can be used to run pump sets and tractors 
for agriculture use. IIT, Delhi in collaboration with M/s Escorts Ltd., 
Faridabad have demonstrated the utilization of bio-diesel with diesel in tractor 
engines. 
(c) and (d) The cost of bio-diesel produced depends on the cost and type of 
non-edible vegetable oil used, plant capacity, type of technology adopted and the 
utilization of byproducts such as glycerine, bio-fertilizers and bio-pesticides, etc. 
Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources, has informed that it may not be 
appropriate to make any projections for the cost of bio-diesel produced on 
commercial scale on the basis of the project which is still in the research and 
development stage

2648. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:

Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to

243 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
and Training (NCERT) and whether NCERT has failed to achieve the 
physical targets fixed for it for the Ninth Plan; and 
(b) if so, what are the reasons therefor and the steps taken by NCERT to 
achieve its targets? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) and (b) the objects of 
the Council are to assist and advise the Government of India on academic matters 
related to school education. The aims and objectives of the NCERT, in particular, 
include: 
(i) To undertake aid, promote and coordinate research in all branches of 
education; 
(ii) To organize pre-service and in-service training; 
(iii) To organize extension services for such institutions as are engaged in 
educational research, training of teachers or provision of extension services to 
school; 
(iv) To develop and/or to disseminate improved educational techniques and 
practices in schools; 
(v) To cooperate with, collaborate and assist the State Education 
Departments, Universities and other educational institutions for the 
furtherance of its objects; 
(vi) To advise the State Governments and other educational organizations and 
institutions on matters relating to school education. 
(vii) To undertake the preparation and or the publication of such books, 
Materials; Periodicals an d other literature as may be necessary for the 
furtherance of its objects. 
(viii) To act as a clearing-house for ideas and information on all matters 
relating to school education. 
The NCERT has intimated that it was able to spend 78% of the funds 
sanctioned during the Ninth Plan period. The shortfall of 22% was due to delay 
in the completion of the construction works of the proposed building for the 
North-East Regional Institute of Ed ucation (NERIE) at Shillong. However, 
during the first two years of the Tenth Five year Plan NCERT has been able to 
achieve the physical targets fixed for it.

RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether his Ministry has sent a note to the CMs of the States which are lagging 
behind in implementation of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan; 
(b) if so, details of such States and their reaction thereto;

253 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
(d) if so, whether Government are considering to monitor progress of 
implementation of this scheme by such States;

above communication; and

the scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMi): (a) to (f) The Minister 
for Human Resource Development had written a letter on 23rd October, 2004

IIT status to engineering colleges 
  2654.   SHRI R. SHUNMUGASUNDARAM:                          
SHRI S.ANBALAGAN:                                             
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government would accord IIT status to the engineering 
colleges already given Deemed University status in Tamil Nadu; 
(b) what are the criteria for giving IIT status; and 
(c) how many colleges in the country would be given such status? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) No, Sir. 
(b) and (c) With a view to identify promising academic institutions, to be 
upgraded into Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) an Expert Committee under the 
Chairmanship of Prof. S.K. Joshi was constituted and was given a mandate for 
considering the proposals for upgrada tion of academic institutes/universities 
and their conversion into IITs. 
The Committee, after considering factors which are used in the evaluation 
257 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
of technical Institutions by AICTE, arrived at benchmarks for parameters such 
as Faculty, Research Publications/Patents, Research Guidance, Courses 
offered, student population, physical infrastructure, Geographical Location and 
its advantages/disadvantages etc. in order to shortlist ins titutions having 
potential for upgradation to NTs. Though the Committee has identified a few 
institutes possessing the best potential among the Engineering and Technology 
Colleges in the country for upgradation to the level of NTs, it feels that there exists a 
substantial gap between the selected institutes and NTs.. 
The Committee were, therefore, of the view that before taking the final 
decision on their recommendations, the Ministry of HRD may like to set up a 
small expert group that would need to visit the identified Institutions to assess 
their suitability and also to assess, first hand, the problems of transformation of 
these institutions to NT like institutes. The group can then also arrive at the 
quantum of one time financial support needed for managing such a 
transformation of the institutions in the event the government decides to 
upgrade any of them.

Women living in bigamous wedlocks 
      2656.   SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA:                      
SHRI N.K. PREMACHANDRAN: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether despite all legal provisions to the contrary data on marital status released 
recently reveals that about 6.4 million Indians below 18 years of age are already married and 
about 10 million women in the country are living in bigamous wedlocks; 
(b) if so, Government's response thereto; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI KANTI SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. As per Census of India, 
2001, there are 6.4 million Indians under the age of 18 years, who are reported to be already 
married. At the national level the number of married women exceed the number of 
married men by 5 million. 
(b) and (c) The Government has taken serious note of the report. Though bigamy is an 
offence punishable under Indian Penal Code, the Government has taken several steps to 
eliminate child marriages from the country. Such as, 
 State Governments have been asked for strict implementation of Child Marriage 
(Restraint) Act, 1929. 
 State Governments have been asked to take necessary measures to prevent child 
marriages in their States. 
 The proposal for amendment to the Child Marriage (Restraint) Act, 1929 is 
presently under consideration of the Government which would help in better 
implementation of the Act. 
 NHRC is also taking steps at its level to address the issue. 
 A strong media campaign is being launched by the Department of Women and Child 
Development especially to target prevention of child marriages in the forthcoming 
festival season of Akshaya Teej. 
 During 2002-03 and 2003-04, the National Commission for Women 
262 

[19 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
launched Bal Vivah Virodh Abhiyan and in 2004-05 the Commission has 
asked the State Governments to take  steps to curb child marriages. 
The Commission is also collabora ting with State Governments and 
State Women Commissions for launching the Bal Vivah Virodh Abhiyan 
and putting efforts to generate awareness against this social evil. 
Foreign lnvestment in higher education 
  2657.   DR. KARAN SINGH: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether present Government are open to allow foreign investment in higher 
education; 
(b) if so, whether Government have had a detailed consultation with all the 
stake holders before taking any final decision in this regard; 
(c) if so, by when a final decision is likely to be taken in this regard; 
 
(d) whether a conference of the State Education Ministers and Secretaries 
was held in January in Bangalore; 
(e) if so, whether this question was also discussed; and 
(f) if so, what were the other decisions taken in the conference? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (f) Foreign Direct 
Investment (FDI) in Education, including higher education, is already being 
allowed under the automatic route, with out any sectoral cap, since February, 
2000 vide Order No. 7(4)/2000-IP dated 11th February, 2000 issued by the 
Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion. 
In order to consult the State Governments on the subject of regulating 
admissions and fixation of fee for professional education through self 
financing private institutions as well as entry of foreign universities in India, a 
conference of State Ministers of Higher and Technical Education was organised 
at Bangalore on January 10-11,2005. While, there is no specific directive in this 
regard, however, in the Conference a broad consensus was arrived at on the 
need for a Central Legislation in this regard. A draft bill has been prepared for 
vetting by the concerned Departments and 
263 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
circulation among various stakeholders including State Governments, to elicit their views 
for eliminating arbitrariness and malpratices in professional educational institutions. 
Acommittee of experts has been set up in regard to all issues pertaining to the entry of 
foreign universities in India.

     2658.   SHRIMATI JAMANA DEVI BARUPAL:                      
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY:                                       
SHRI DATTA MEGHE: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether statistics of a nationwide survey conducted in June and August, 2004 
and presented to the Planning Commission by an organization working on 
elementary education has pointed out that 19 per cent of girls drop out of schools by age of 14 
and an average 25 per cent of all school children cannot write a dictated sentence by that 
age; 
(b) if so, whether according to the findings about 29 per cent boys and 33 per cent girls 
were out of schools in age group of 11 and 14; 
(c) if so, what are the other points mentioned in the report; and 
(d) to what extent Government have considered the survey report? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) and (b) As per information 
received from Planning Commission, an organization working in elementary education had 
made a presentation to it regarding a sample survey on "Rapid Assessment of Learning 
Outcomes" conducted by it in June-August, 2004, covering 17 States and about 13,500 
children. The survey results based on preliminary analysis showed; inter-alia, that:— 
(i) 25% of children of 11-14 years age group in Government schools, and 14% in 
private schools, were unable to write a dictated sentence, and 
(ii) 8% of the boys and 18% of girls in the age group 11-14 years were out of 
school. 
(c) The report indicated that the "Learning to Read" programme introduced by the 
organization resulted in significantly enhanced reading levels among children, particularly 
in remote, tribal and backward areas. 
(d) Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan programme aims to address the concerns 
264 

[19 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
raised in the report through various measures aimed at improving enrolment, 
retention and learning. 
Women Trafficking from Nepal and Bangladesh 
   2659.   SHRI TARINI KANTA ROY: 
SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that women trafficking from Nepal and 
Bangladesh is on the increase; and 
(b) if so, what action is being taken by Government to stop this menace? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI KANTI SINGH): (a) The Government is aware of 
the existence of the problem of women trafficking from Nepal and 
Bangladesh through India. 
(b) Trafficking of Women in one of the agents items in various institutional 
mechanisms between India and Nepal to deal with cross-border security related 
issues. These include Joint Working Group on Border Management, Interpol 
Officers, Meetings and Border District Co-ordination Committees involving 
District Magistrates/Chief Development Officers and other officials of districts on 
both sides of the Indo-Nepal border. 
The issue of trafficking of women and children has been discussed with 
Bangladesh in the DG level BSF-BDR talks in 2004 and also during the Home 
Secretary level talks held between India and Bangladesh. 
The Government of India has signed and ratified SAARC Convention on 
Prevention and Combating Trafficking in Women and Children for 
Prosititution.

2665. SHRI R.P GOENKA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the S.K. Joshi Committee, set up to study a 
proposal to start five new IITs in different States, has submitted its report; 
(b) if so, the details of the major recommendations made by the 
Committee and the action taken/proposed to be taken thereon; 
(c) whether the Committee has suggested any fresh guidelines to evaluate the 
academic standing and infrastructure of an institute for its upgradation to the 
status of and "IIT"; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALIASHRAF FATMI): (a) Yes, Sir. (b) to (d) 
The Committee, after considering factors which are used in the evaluation of 
technical Institutions by AICTE, arrived at benchmarks for parameters such as 
Faculty, Research Publications/Patents, Research Guidance, Course offered, 
student population, physical infrastructure, Geographical Locations and its 
advantages/disadvantages etc. in orde r to shortlist institutions having the 
potential for upgradation to IITs. Though the Committee has identified a few 
institutes possessing the best potential among the Engineering & Tec hnology 
Colleges in the country for upgradation to the level of IITs, it feels that there exists a 
substantial gap between the selected institutes and IITs. No fresh guidelines were 
suggested. 
The Committee were, therefore, of the view that before taking the final 
decision on their recommendations, the Ministry of HRD may like to set up a 
small expert group that would need to visit the identified Institutions to assess at 
their suitability and also to assess, first hand, the problems of transformation of 
these Institutions to NT like Institutes, the group can then also arrive at the

Statement 
The details of various Commissions working under the Administrative control 
of the Ministry of HRD 
I. National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions 
The Composition of the Commission for Minority Educational Institutions is 
Chairman and two Members with the tenure period of Five Years. The date of 
constitution of the Commission is 11th November, 2004. The criteria laid down for 
nomination of Chairpersons and Members is as under: 
i. The Chairperson of the Commission shall be a Member of the Minority 
Community and should have been a Judge of a High Court; and 
ii. The Members shall be from a Minority Community and persons of 
eminence, ability and integrity. 
Presently, no vacancies exist in the Commission. 
II. Indian National Commission for Cooperation with UNESCO (INCCU) 
The Indian National Commission for Cooperation with UNESCO (INCCU) 
comprises Members of five Sub-Commissions covering the sectors of 
UNESCO's competence namely (1) Education (2) Culture (3) Natural 
Sciences (4) Social Sciences and (5 ) Communication. Each Sub-Commission 
consist of not more than ten individual and ten Institutional members. Members 
hold office for a term of four years. 
The Minister of Human Resource Development is the President of the 
Commission. Individual Members are nominated by the President of the 
Commission in their personal capacity  from amongst eminent educationists, 
scientists, persons distinguished in the field of social sciences, humanities, 
culture and communication. Institutional Members comprise 
289 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
the concerned Government Departments, important statutory and 
autonomous bodies, national professional organizations and national non-
governmental bodies concerned with or working for education, natural 
sciences, social sciences, humanities, culture and communication. 
Against the maximum strength of hundred, at present there are 60    members 
in the Commission. 
III. University Grants Commission (UGC) 
The University Grants Commission comprises a Chairman, a Vice-
Chairman and ten other members. Appointments of the Chairman, Vice-
Chairman and other Members of the Commission are made in accordance with 
Section 5 and 6 of the UGC Act. The tenure of appointment of Chairman is 5 years 
and that of Vice-Chairman and other Members is 3 years. At present, there is 
no vacancy in the Commission. 
IV. National Commission for Women (NCW) 
The National Commission for Women consists of a Chairperson, five   -
Members and a Member-Secretary. The tenure of the Chairperson and each 
member is for a period of three years or till they attain the age of 65, whichever is 
earlier. 
The criteria laid down for nominating the Chairperson and Members is given 
in section 3 of the National Commission for Women Act, 1990. At present, 
there are two vacancies of Members in  the Commission and action to fill up 
these vacancies has been initiated in accordance with the prescribed 
procedure.

303

JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Details are given in the Statement (See below)

1247.00 lakhs under Plan and Rs. 2397.00 lakhs under Non-Plan.

(d) and (e) The role of Films Division indicated in the Annexure in reply to

Because of the provisions for compulsory screening of 'approved' films by

showcased for the future generation. The films of Films Division are also 
being telecast on National Network and other Regional Channels of

Statement 
Role of the Films Division 
Films Division is responsible for production and distribution of 
documentaries, animation and short films required by the Government of India 
for public information, education, and motivation and for instructional 
304 

[19 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and cultural purposes. By supplying 'approved films', Films Division helps Cinema exhibitors 
to fulfil the statutory obligation requiring exhibition of such films under the provisions 
contained in the Cinematograph Act, 1952 and various State Laws. Films Division gives a 
fillip to the growth of documentary film movement in India. Apart from producing films 
through its own units, Films Division also gets films produced through independent producers 
so as to encourage them to express their creativity. Apart from ' participating in National and 
International Film Festivals, the Division organizes the biennial Mumbai 
International Film Festival (MIFF), a prestigious competitive Film Festival 
exclusively devoted for documentary, short and animation films, now recognized at 
par with the topmost international film festivals like Leipzig, Berlin, Oberhausen, 
Cracow, Tampere etc. Films Division has a treasure trove of archive films, which it 
also retails, on demand. By virtue of its continued coverage of the journey of the 
nation in the social, cultural, economic and political fields, it has a unique collection 
of more than 8000 films and this priceless treasure has become an invaluable 
source of reference. Films Division has started transferring its archival films from 
celluloid to video formats like VCD and DVD to preserve it for posterity and for 
future on-line transfer Internet and other e-modes.

specialists/experts in this field? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF MINES (DR. DASARI 
NARAYANA RAO): (a) and (b) Geologica l Survey of India (GSI) is not 
directly involved in the safety aspects of the people living in the coastal areas. 
However, GSI is one of the members in the Department of Science and Technology 
(DST) Committee on resettlement issues as a sequel to the Tsunami in 
Andaman and Nicobar region. 
GSI has taken immediate action for carrying out multifarious 
geoscientific studies on the aftermath of the devastating earthquake and Tsunami 
of 26th December 2004 as detailed below— 
(i)    A team of scientists led by the Director General, GSI visited South 
Andaman and Baratang Islands to study the effects of earthquake 
332 

[19 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and Tsunami. Preliminary results of this study has already been communicated to 
Andaman and Nicobar Administration and other organizations involved in 
similar studies. 
(ii) Several teams from GSI have carried out detailed scientific studies in the Andaman 
group of islands after the earthquake. These include Macro-seismic (post 
earthquake damage survey to constrain earthquake intensity) survey, Global 
Positioning System (GPS) survey in campaing mode for constraining 
ground deformation, study of aftershocks with five digital seismographs 
deployed in the islands at Port Blair, carnic (Car Nicobar), Hut Bay (Little 
Andaman), Rangat (Middle Andaman) and Diglipur (North Andaman). Nearly 6500 
aftershocks have been recorded by GSI, which show a trend of continuous release 
of stress energy. 
(iii) Teams of Geoscientists from GSI have carried out studies on the effects of 
Tsunami (post - Tsunami survey) in the coastal tract of Andhra Pradesh, 
Tamil Nadu and Kerala. 
(iv) To study the changes in the offshore domain, GSI has undertaken Bathymetry and 
magnetic surveys out in the sea around Andaman and Nicobar islands to study the 
submarine geomorphological changes. 
(v) GSI has posted all relevant information and data on its Website i.e. 
www.gsi.gov.in and this website is being continuously updated. 
(vi) During 25th to 27th January, 2005, GSI members alongwith other DST 
Committee Members visited Port Blair in connection with collection of data 
on submergence/re-settlement issues in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. 
The expert team studied run up/ submergence/inundation problem in the 
area.

field.

2732. SHRI T.T.V DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE 
AND EMPOWERMENT (SHRIMATI SUBBULAKSHMI JAGADEESAN):(a) 
No such report has been received. 
(b) and (c) The following schemes are under implementation for providing 
education to the children with disabilities:- 
(i) Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) has a goal of eight years of elementary

providing integrated and inclusive education to the children with 
special needs in general schools. The

integrated education in schools by providing 100% financial assistance for

(a) The Constitution was amended in December, 2002 for making free and compulsory 
education, a Fundamental Right for all children in the age group of 6-14 years. Accordingly, 
a national programme for Universal Elementary Education viz. Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
(SSA) was launched by the M/o Human Resource Development. It has the goal of eight 
years of elementary schooling for all children including children with disabilities in the 
age-group of 6-14 years by 2010. Under the scheme, a shelf of education options, 
learning aid and tool, mobility assistance, support services etc. are available for 
children with disabilities. Likewise augmentation of teaching skills and capabilities of 
teachers are also made available under the scheme. 
(b) The Department of Secondary Education under Ministry of Human Resource 
Development undertakes a Scheme for the Integrated Education of the Disabled Children 
(IEDC) through Education Departments of the State Governments, Autonomous Bodies 
and Voluntary Organisations. Under the scheme of IEDC 100% financial assistance is 
provided for transport facility, books and stationery, uniform, instructional material, 
assistive equipments, readers facility for the visually handicapped, attendant facility for the 
children with locomotor disability, special teacher facilities, hostel facility for disabled 
children in the school campus, removal of architectural barries in schools etc. 
(c) The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment supports 657 institutions for 
running early intervention programmes, special education programmes, vocational 
training programmes, teachers training programmes in special education, etc. 
350 

[19 April, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) National Trust for the Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Mental 
Retardation and Multiple Disabilities provides training to care-givers for imparting 
home-based life-skill training to the children with severe and profound disabilities. 
(e) Rehabilitation Council of India has recognized training programmes for the training 
of master trainers for teachers in primary schools as a part of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan 
(SSA). It has also recognized B.Ed. (Special Education) for training of teachers is 
special schools. This programme is implemented through National Institutes, private 
institutions and through distance learning. 
(f) Scholarship is provided to the children with mental retardation and Cerebral Palsy 
under the Scheme of National Welfare Fund. 
(g) Funds are provided for fitment of aids and appliances to the children with 
disabilities covered under SSA. 
(h) All the textbooks prescribed by NCERT have been printed in Braille for 
children with visual disabilities. 
(i) The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment in pursuance of the provisions of 
Section 30 of the Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995 has notified guidelines dated 
4.11.2004 for the preparation of education scheme for persons with disabilities for 
implementation by the Central Ministries, organizations and autonomous bodies under their 
control. These guidelines have also been circulated to the State Governments for suitable 
adoption keeping in view their local requirements. 
(j) The Government has formulated a comprehensive Action Plan for the Inclusive 
Education of Children and Youth with Disabilities. 
The implementation of the provisions of the Act is being undertaken with a 
multisectoral collaborative approach by the concerned Ministries/ Departments of the 
Central Government, the State Governments and other appropriate authorities. They 
continue to take steps towards effective implementation of the various provisions of the 
Act, including the provisions relating to children with disabilities.

to reserve minimum three per cent seats for the physically challenged persons;

Semi Pornography in Electronic and Print Media 
2760. SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of increasing semi pornography in 
electronic and print media ;and 
(b) if so, the steps Government propose to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) and (b) Prasar Bharati has Programme and Advertising Codes 
which inter-alia, prohibit telecast/broadcast of any programme or 
advertisement, which contains anything obscene. Doordarshan and All India 
Radio abide by the codes while telecasting/broadcasting their programmes. 
The Programmes of all Satellite Channels, when transmitted/ 
retransmitted through cable television networks in the country, are required to 
adhere to the Programmes and Advertising Codes prescribed under the Cable 
Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 and Rules framed thereunder. 
The Programme Code prohibits carriage of such programmes in Cable Service, 
which offend good taste or decency, c ontain anything obscene or denigrates 
women through the depiction in any manner of the figure of a women, her form or 
body or any part thereof in such a way as to have the effect of being indecent, or 
derogatory to women or is likely to deprave, corrupt or injure the public 
morality or morals, contravenes the provisions of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 and 
is not suitable for unrestricted public exhibition. 
373 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
Action for violations of the codes can be taken by any authorized officer i.e. 
SDM, DM or Commissioner of Police or any other officer notified in the official gazette by 
the Central Government or State Government. 
The Central Government has constituted two inter-ministerial Committees 
under Section 20 of the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 to look into the 
violations of the Programme and Advertising Code. 
The Government has decided to set up a Broadcasting Content Regulatory 
Authority to receive and dispose of complaints on content telecast on TV channels. A 
Core Group has already been set up in the Ministry to deliberate and draft the Bill 
in this regard. 
In so far as the Print Media is concerned, the Government does not interfere in 
the matters relating to the Press. The Press Council of India (PCI) is a statutory authority 
established for preserving the freedom of the Press and for maintaining and improving the 
standards of newspapers and news agencies in India. PCI has set the Norms for Journalists 
Conduct according to which Newspapers/journalists shall not publish anything which is 
obscene, vulgar or offensive to public good taste. 
The publishing of obscene and nude/semi nude photographs of women is an 
offence under Section 3 of the Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986 
which is administered by the Department of Women and Child Development, 
Ministry of Human Resource Development.

Water supply in slums and colonies in NCT of Delhi 
2765. SHRI E. M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN: Will the Minister of 
URBAN DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that basic in frastructure of water supply is not 
available in various slum and small colonies in the NCT of Delhi and people are 
forced to take impure and disease-prone water; and 
(b) if so, what steps are being taken by Government to provide potable water 
in these areas? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI GHULAM NABI 
AZAD): (a) and (b) Slum & JJ Department of Municipal Corporation of Delhi 
has reported that infrastructure for water supply is available in all the resettlement 
pockets developed by them. 
Delhi Jal Board (DJB) has reported that mostly water supply in slum 
colonies is through public water hydrants, Deep Bore Hand Pumps (DBHPs) 
and Tube wells. In case of shortage of water, the same is supplemented by 
supplying drinking water through tankers. Regular sampling is done by DJB 
to ensure the quality of water. 
387 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2005] 
Pressure on civic amenities in Metropolitan cities 
2766. SHRI T. T. V. DHINAKAR AN: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the metropolitan cities are facing increased shortage 
of water, power etc., as a result of growing population; 
(b) if so, the steps proposed to be taken to handle the situation; and 
(c) the steps taken/proposed to be taken to discourage migration to metropolis 
from the rural areas? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD): 
(a) to (c) Yes, Sir. In order to provide reform linked Central assistance for 
development of infrastructure, including water supply, in all cities/towns of the 
country, there is a proposal for National Urban Renewal Mission for select cities and 
Urban Infrastructure Development Scheme for Small and Medium Towns. Details in 
this regard have not been finalized.

development under progress in Chennai; and

constructions in the private colonies under this Plan?

2780. SHRI C. PERUMAL: Will the Minister of URBAN EMPLOYMENT

employment oriented Urban Poverty Alleviation Centrally sponsored scheme named 
Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY), on all India basis, with effect
